name: Roman Empire (117) vs Spain (2026)
description: Rome at its peak under Trajan against modern Spain, fought in Iberia, each side with its own era's technology.

name: Mongol Empire (1241) vs Napoleonic France (1805)
description: The Mongol invasion force against the Grande Armee in Central Europe.

name: Allies vs Axis without the two largest nations
description: World War II with the USA and USSR (the two largest economies, Maddison GDP 1940) removed: Britain and France against Germany, Italy and Japan in Europe.

name: Achaemenid Persia vs the Greek city-states (480 BCE)
description: Xerxes' invasion of Greece against the Hellenic League.

name: United States vs China (2026)
description: Modern superpower war in the Western Pacific. Nuclear weapons off by default.

name: Rome (117) vs Napoleonic France, tech equalized
description: Both sides given Napoleonic-era technology (level 6): population, economy, geography and doctrine stay their own.

name: Germany vs France (1940)
description: The 1940 Western campaign as a free-play scenario: German mobile warfare against the French methodical defence.

name: Macedon (334 BCE) vs Achaemenid Persia (480 BCE), time-slice
description: Alexander's army against Xerxes' empire at its height: a mixed-year hypothetical.

name: USA and Spain vs Russia (2026)
description: A NATO-Russia war in Eastern Europe with the two NATO members in the slice (more members in Phase 2).

name: Japan vs United States (1941)
description: The Pacific War from December 1941.

name: Mongol Empire (1241) vs Roman Empire (117)
description: Steppe mobility against Roman legions and engineering, fought in the Balkans and Danube.

name: Athens (480 BCE) vs United States (2026)
description: Absurd pairing kept as a stress test: the model must run and explain a 2,500-year tech gap.

name: Roman Republic vs Carthage (218 BCE)
description: The Second Punic War at its outbreak: the Roman Republic against Barcid Carthage and its Iberian holdings, fought across Italy, Iberia and North Africa. Both snapshots are grade C, so the result is low-confidence model output, not a replay of what happened.

name: Han dynasty (100 BCE) vs Xiongnu (200 BCE), time-slice
description: Steppe horse archers against the Han state on the northern frontier: the Xiongnu confederation at its early height against the Western Han after Emperor Wu's reforms. A mixed-year hypothetical; both snapshots are grade C, so treat the outcome as low-confidence model output.

theater.name: Northern China and the Mongolian steppe

name: Neo-Assyria (670 BCE) vs Kush (700 BCE), time-slice
description: Esarhaddon's Assyria against the Kushite pharaohs who ruled Egypt, fought over the Levant and the Nile delta. The Kush snapshot is from 700 BCE, a generation before the historical clash. Both are grade C: low-confidence model output, not a reconstruction of the 671 BCE campaign.

name: Napoleonic France (1805) vs the Third Coalition
description: The 1805 campaign in Central Europe: the Grande Armee against Austria, Russia and Britain. Russia and Britain use their nearest snapshots (1812 and 1815), so this is a time-slice. All four snapshots are grade C; the outcome is low-confidence model output and does not predict Ulm or Austerlitz.

name: Central Powers vs Entente (1914)
description: The opening of World War I in Europe on both fronts: Germany and Austria-Hungary against France, Britain and Russia. The Ottoman Empire (entered November 1914), Italy, Serbia and Belgium are not in the scenario. All snapshots are grade C: low-confidence model output, not a forecast of the 1914 campaigns.

name: NATO vs Warsaw Pact (1989)
description: The Cold War hypothetical that never happened: the United States, Britain, France and West Germany against the Soviet Union and East Germany in Central Europe. Poland, Czechoslovakia and the other Pact and NATO members have no 1989 snapshot yet. Nuclear weapons off. All snapshots are grade C: low-confidence model output.

name: India vs Pakistan (1971)
description: The December 1971 war on both fronts, West Pakistan and East Pakistan. The Bengali insurgency (Mukti Bahini) and the naval blockade politics are not modelled separately. Both snapshots are grade C: low-confidence model output; the historical war ended in 13 days and the model is not expected to reproduce that.

name: North Korea vs South Korea (1950)
description: The June 1950 invasion with the Korean peninsula left to the two Korean states: neither the UN intervention nor China's entry is in the scenario. Both snapshots are grade C, so the result is low-confidence model output about a counterfactual, not the war as fought.

name: Mali Empire (1330) vs Songhai Empire (1500), time-slice
description: The two great Sahelian empires at their heights, fought along the Niger bend in the dry campaigning season: Mansa Musa's Mali against Askia Muhammad's Songhai. They never met at these strengths. Both snapshots are low grade C: treat the outcome as low-confidence model output.

name: Japan (1600) vs Joseon Korea (1592), time-slice
description: The Imjin War setting: a Japanese invasion across the Korea Strait against Joseon Korea in 1592, where the landing depends on the fight for the strait. Japan uses the nearest snapshot (Tokugawa, 1600), and Ming China's intervention is not in the scenario. Both snapshots are grade C: low-confidence model output, not a replay of the 1592-98 war.

name: Roman Empire (117) vs Ottoman Empire (1566), tech equalized
description: Two empires that ruled the same Mediterranean lands 1,450 years apart, both given early-gunpowder technology (level 5): population, economy, geography and doctrine stay their own. Overlapping land starts contested. A cross-era what-if; both snapshots are grade C, so the result is low-confidence model output.

name: Argentina vs United Kingdom (1982)
description: The Falklands War from April 1982 in the South Atlantic: a task force operating 12,000 km from home against an air force and navy fighting near their own coast. Both snapshots are grade C and the islands are not in Argentina's border polygon (Stanley is a place only), so the outcome is low-confidence model output.
